lead: EEG and EMG look similar on a screen but come from different scales. EEG records summed postsynaptic potentials of cortical neurons, often 10–100 microvolts (µV), through scalp electrodes. EMG records action potentials of muscle fibres, often 0.1–5 millivolts (mV), through surface or needle electrodes. EMG is typically 20–50 times larger than EEG (10–500 times across the full ranges), so each branch needs its own gain, band and filter. EEG uses gain near 10⁴ and a 0.5–70 Hz band; EMG uses lower gain, often 10²–10³, and a 20–500 Hz band. Clinics use these recordings for brain state, muscle activation and fatigue checks. Remember 1 mV = 1000 µV; check units before choosing gain.
prereq: You need: resting and action potentials for resting and action potentials, electrode theory for electrode impedance, and bio-amplifiers and data acquisition for differential gain and CMRR.

blocks.text: Cortical neurons communicate through postsynaptic potentials. A single potential is tiny, but millions of aligned pyramidal cells sum at the scalp. The result is the electroencephalogram (EEG), a random-looking wave of 10–100 µV. EEG is used for sleep staging, anaesthesia depth and seizure monitoring; seizure detail is in multichannel EEG and evoked potentials.

Scalp electrodes follow the 10–20 system. Names mark the brain region: Fp frontopolar, F frontal, C central, P parietal, O occipital, T temporal. Odd numbers are left, even numbers right, and z is midline. Fp1, F3, C3, P3 and O1 form a left-side chain; Fp2, F4, C4, P4 and O2 mirror it on the right. A1 and A2 are earlobe references.

A referential montage connects each active electrode to one common reference, such as an earlobe or the average of all electrodes. It shows activity spread over the scalp. A bipolar montage connects adjacent electrodes, for example Fp1–F3. It rejects common noise and sharpens local differences, but it needs more channels.

items: Delta: below 4 Hz; deep sleep (slow eye movements can imitate it).
Alpha: 8–13 Hz; relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.
Beta: 13–30 Hz; active thinking and some drugs.
Gamma: above 30 Hz; small, and easily confused with muscle activity.

blocks.text: EEG gain is about 10⁴ because 50 µV × 10⁴ = 0.5 V, a useful ADC range. The band 0.5–70 Hz passes delta to beta and removes slow sweat drift and high-frequency muscle. A 50 Hz notch removes mains interference in India. Sampling at 250 Hz gives a Nyquist frequency of 125 Hz, above the 70 Hz band. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter set near 70–100 Hz still goes before the ADC, so noise and muscle activity above 125 Hz never fold into the EEG band.

Eye blinks appear as slow frontal waves, jaw clench adds EMG, loose electrodes give pops, and sweat drifts the baseline. Checking electrode impedance and asking the patient to relax the jaw removes many faults.

EMG records the electrical activity of muscle fibres. A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it drives. When the neuron fires, the fibre action potentials sum into a motor unit action potential (MUAP). Surface electrodes on the skin over the muscle belly and a tendon record many MUAPs together. Needle electrodes enter the muscle and pick up single units with better selectivity, but they are invasive.

Surface EMG is in the millivolt range, roughly 0.1–5 mV; needle EMG can reach several millivolts. A smaller gain than EEG is enough, often 10²–10³. The band is 20–500 Hz because MUAP edges are fast. The amplifier still needs high common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), and a 50 Hz notch removes mains. Sample above 1 kHz so the Nyquist frequency is above 500 Hz.

Raw EMG is zero-mean and oscillatory, so one number needs a processing chain. Filter first with the band-pass and 50 Hz notch filters. Then rectify: take the absolute value |x(t)|. After that choose one amplitude measure. Low-pass smooth the rectified signal to get the mean absolute (averaged rectified) value, or compute RMS over a window directly from the filtered or rectified signal. Do not apply RMS after smoothing; RMS already does the averaging.

blocks.where: x(t) is the filtered EMG voltage in volts; T is the averaging window in seconds; x<sub>RMS</sub> is the root mean square in volts.

blocks.text: In a sustained contraction, fatigue shifts the EMG spectrum downward: the median frequency falls. Amplitude often rises first as more motor units are recruited, then falls as fibres tire. The frequency shift is the more reliable fatigue sign.

The two branches must not share one gain and one filter. EEG at 50 µV through EMG gain 10³ gives only 0.05 V, a small fraction of the ADC range, so resolution is poor and the gain error shows. EMG at 2 mV through EEG gain 10⁴ gives 20 V, which clips the amplifier. Use separate plug-in modules or software presets; label them clearly. Run a short routine before trusting a trace.

items: Check each electrode impedance before recording; a high impedance picks up 50 Hz and movement.
Ask the patient to blink, clench and relax; identify artefacts in the record.
Test the 50 Hz notch and the calibration pulse at the start and end of a session.
Record a known calibration signal before each session; a gain error changes every later reading.
For EMG, mark the contraction level and joint angle; RMS depends on both.
For EEG, keep the reference consistent; changing reference changes the waveform.

examples.question: An EEG amplifier has gain 10,000 and input 50 µV. What is the output? If the EEG is sampled at 250 Hz, what is the Nyquist frequency?
steps: Convert the input: 50 µV = 50 × 10⁻⁶ V = 5 × 10⁻⁵ V.
Find the output: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × A = 5 × 10⁻⁵ V × 10,000 = 0.5 V.
Find the Nyquist frequency: fN = fs ÷ 2 = 250 Hz ÷ 2 = 125 Hz.
Check the band: 125 Hz is above the 70 Hz EEG upper limit, so the sampled EEG does not alias.
examples.answer: The output is 0.5 V and the Nyquist frequency is 125 Hz.
examples.check:
gain = 10000
vin_uV = 50
vout_V = vin_uV * 1e-6 * gain
fs_Hz = 250
nyquist_Hz = fs_Hz / 2
print(vout_V)
print(int(nyquist_Hz))

examples.question: Four successive samples of a filtered surface EMG are 0.4, −0.8, 1.2 and −0.4 mV. (a) Find the mean absolute value and the RMS of this window. (b) During a 60 s held contraction the median frequency falls from 120 Hz to 84 Hz. Find the percentage fall and say what it shows.
steps: RMS = √0.60 = 0.775 mV. RMS is larger than the mean absolute value because squaring weights the big 1.2 mV sample more.
A 30 % downward shift of the spectrum is the classic sign of muscle fatigue: conduction along the tiring fibres slows, so power moves to lower frequencies.
examples.answer: Mean absolute value 0.70 mV and RMS 0.775 mV; the median frequency falls by 30 %, which shows fatigue.

traps: µV and mV are not interchangeable. EEG is 10–100 µV; surface EMG is 0.1–5 mV. A 1000× slip changes the gain choice.
Using EEG gain 10⁴ on EMG clips the amplifier; using EMG gain 10³ on EEG gives a small output and poor ADC resolution.
A bipolar montage does not mean a reference to earth. It measures the difference between two scalp electrodes, so common noise cancels.

Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, not the sampling rate itself. Sampling at 250 Hz gives 125 Hz, not 250 Hz. A high Nyquist frequency is not enough by itself; an anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the ADC stops higher-frequency noise folding back.
Fatigue is not only a smaller signal. The median frequency falls, and amplitude can rise first before it falls.

quiz.q: State the four main EEG bands and their frequency limits.
quiz.a: Delta below 4 Hz, theta 4–8 Hz, alpha 8–13 Hz, beta 13–30 Hz.

quiz.q: Why does EEG need about 10⁴ gain while EMG does not?
quiz.a: EEG is only 10–100 µV, so high gain lifts it to about 0.1–1 V. Surface EMG is 0.1–5 mV, typically 20–50 times larger (10–500 times across the full ranges), so the same gain would clip it. A lower gain, often 10²–10³, is enough.

quiz.q: A surface EMG signal of 2 mV is amplified by 500. What is the output voltage?
During a sustained contraction, median EMG frequency falls from 120 Hz to 80 Hz and RMS rises by 20%. What does this suggest?
quiz.a: The frequency drop and RMS rise suggest muscle fatigue. More motor units are recruited while fibre conduction slows, shifting power to lower frequencies.
A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a referential and a bipolar EEG montage.
quiz.a: A referential montage compares each active electrode with one common reference. A bipolar montage compares adjacent electrodes, so it rejects common noise but needs more channels.

quiz.q: An EEG is sampled at 200 Hz. What is the Nyquist frequency? Is a 70 Hz EEG band safe from aliasing?
quiz.a: Nyquist frequency = 200 Hz ÷ 2 = 100 Hz. The 70 Hz band is below 100 Hz, so the band itself does not alias. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the ADC handles higher-frequency noise.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern EEG uses dry or gel-free electrodes and wearable headsets for long recordings outside a clinic. EMG is moving into wearable bands for sports, rehabilitation and fatigue monitoring, where machine learning classifies the frequency shift. Brain-computer interfaces use EEG bands, while prosthetic hands use EMG from remaining muscles. Search for dry EEG electrodes, surface EMG fatigue, and EMG-controlled prosthetics.
